subject: seahorse
pitch: A lined seahorse holding on to a strand of seagrass with its curled tail. A ridged body in sunny yellow with thin dark lines and a few white freckles, a little crown of spikes on its head, a long tube snout, a delicate fluttering fin on its back, and big, curious eyes.
reasoning:
I'm scaling the model realistically, with the seagrass strand setting the overall height and the seahorse around 0.18m, resting on a small sand or rock base at y=0. I'm planning the spine as a chain starting from the head to build the seahorse's curved posture.

I'm positioning the seagrass vertically near z=0 and curling the seahorse's tail in a spiral around that axis, with the upright body and snout facing forward above it. I'm working out the tail as a spiral chain anchored at the body's base, then connecting it to a separate chain running up the trunk to the head.

I'm checking that the spiraling tail radius stays clear of the grass blade it passes near, adjusting the shrinking radius from 0.02 down to 0.004 so there's no visible clipping, and tapering it thicker toward the middle for a more natural curve.

Now I want the single path from neck down through chest and belly to connect smoothly into the spiral's starting point, matching positions and centers so the transition reads as one continuous body. I'm working out the right-hand rotation direction so the spiral's initial tangent lines up correctly with the incoming body curve direction.

Then I'm setting up the spine chain itself, placing a root hips joint and defining the chain of roughly 14 joints running from neck through the body path into the spiral, making sure the first chain joint aligns with where the path actually starts.

Rethinking the split: I'll create two separate paths instead of one concatenated catmull — a body path from head to hips, and a spiral tail path — then build two chains, "spine" (parented to root) and "tail" (parented to the last spine joint), sweeping each independently so the radii match up at the junction with rounded caps to hide the seam.

Estimating body length around 0.28 and tail spiral length around 0.2, giving a junction point at roughly 55% along the full path, computed as the body path's fraction of total length. I'm defining a radius profile that widens from a narrow neck to a bulgier chest and belly, then tapers down through the tail, using keyframe interpolation to blend the cross-section dimensions smoothly along the path.

Now I'm working out the coloring: a yellow body with dark ring-like stripes running around it (using the vertical axis so they wrap correctly), layered with subtle white freckle spots, and a creamy countershaded belly for a lighter underside.

Skipping countershade since the body orientation makes "belly" ambiguous here. For the dorsal ridge, I'm thinking of placing small bony studs or spike rings along the body path at intervals, figuring out the correct clock angle (0 facing world-up) so they sit properly along the back given the body's vertical, descending orientation.

Adding more ridge rings...

Now thinking through tail ridge stations and head placement—attaching the head joint at the neck top, oriented forward-down, with the path starting near the neck and running downward.

Actually, reconsidering hierarchy: the root should be the hips, not the head, so I'm restructuring the chains to branch from hips—spine going up to neck/head, and tail going down—with the body path reorganized to run from tail tip to head so the direction matches properly.

Still defining the chain setup...

Still placing the jaw, snout, and skull geometry...

I'm checking that the S-curve body stays clear of the grass stem it's gripping—verifying radii at the hips and neck so the seahorse's back just grazes the grass without clipping through it at each height along the spine.

Adding more grass blades as flat tapered sweeps with a green gradient, plus extra strands of varying height behind the main one, and a small sandy mound base built as a low lathe dome sinking into the floor.

For the tail, I'm working out a spiral path descending from near the body down to about y=0.05-0.08, tuning turns and pitch so it winds naturally, then balancing overall tail and body length and thickness distribution for proportion.

I'm mapping radius values along the tail-to-body transition, using relative position along the path (rootT) to set thickness at the junction, hips, belly, chest, neck, and head, then matching each key point to its closest position on the full curve.

I'm working out an interpolation function for radius that uses elliptical cross-sections (slightly flattened horizontally, bulging for the belly) and smooth blending between keyframes, then thinking through how coat stripe patterns would wrap around the spiraling tail versus the body using a vertical banding approach.

Adding stripe and freckle logic...

Now I'm working out the dorsal fin as a membrane between two swept edge lines along the body's back angle, but I realize the sweep line spans the whole creature's length rather than just the slice I want, so I need to figure out how to trim it to the right section using closest-point matching on the path.

For the fin's appearance, I'm giving it a delicate translucent look with alternating colored rays along its length, painting darker streaks at regular intervals to suggest structure without actually passing a bone reference through the membrane.

Now I'm adding a small pectoral fin near the neck, extruding a thin fan-shaped outline positioned sideways against the body and angled to point backward, treating it as a flat plate oriented in-plane rather than extending forward like the dorsal fin.

I'm designing the eyes now: gold-brown iris spheres with small black pupils and white highlights, positioned symmetrically on either side of the head using the skull's local coordinates, offset outward along the radius so they sit partly embedded in the surface.

Then I'm planning the crown of spikes—a row of five pointed spikes arranged across the top of the skull, computing positions along the skull's surface by azimuth angle so they follow the curve from forehead to back of head.

I'll find the nearest skull hit point near the top-back and ring six spikes around it with radius .014, tilting them 55 degrees so they lean outward and upward like a crown, keeping them uniform for now. Then I'll add smaller nub spikes on the brow and think about the snout and cheeks next.

I'll skip adding separate cheek spines and nostril/mouth details for now, but plan a row of eight small orange spikes along the back ridge from hips to neck, reusing the nodule loop logic with a bigger scale for that angle. For the head pose, I'm working out the neck/head joint direction and local orientation so the head tilts forward along the snout axis correctly.

Now I'm positioning the skull center relative to the head joint, then placing the snout base and tip, lower jaw joint and rod, and upper snout taper, all using local offsets off the head joint with varying radii to shape the gap between upper and lower jaw.

Working out eye placement relative to the head joint using local coordinates for position and a mirrored sideways offset, then figuring out the pupil's aim direction as a local vector.

I'm checking the color palette stays under the paint limit, and working out how the pectoral and dorsal fins attach to the body sweep by sampling closest points and t-values along the skinned surface, including the tail's spiral section.

Now I'm defining the fin edges by slicing the body's contour lines between hip and chest heights, keeping both edges ordered consistently from tail to head, with a thin membrane thickness connecting them. The dorsal fin sits along the upper back with a lifted height profile, possibly scalloped, and I'm considering whether the lift should follow the surface normal for a more natural curve.

For the nodules, I'm placing small cone-shaped spikes at various stations along the body, using a set of angular positions around each cross-section (skipping the belly-facing angle where needed) and scaling their size based on the local body radius at that station, with an orange-ish color for visual texture.

For the tail, I'm using fewer stations and fewer angles since its cross-section is smaller and simpler, keeping only a couple of spike positions along its length.

Now I'm moving on to the grass strands, sweeping a tapered path that narrows toward the tip, giving it a box or circular cross-section, and figuring out which bone or joint near the ground each strand should attach to.

Still tuning grass geometry...

Now I'm designing the sand mound as a lathe shape with a smooth curved outline shrinking from radius .09 at the base to a peak near .028, checking that the tail's spiral end sits comfortably above the mound's surface at each turn.

For the tail-to-hip transition, I need to blend the tail's trailing end into the hip junction smoothly—reversing the tail path so it approaches the hip point moving in the +X direction, then connecting upward into the body curve, using Catmull-Rom interpolation with an added intermediate point to avoid a sharp 90° corner and let the skin round out naturally.

I'm mapping out radius keyframes at each body landmark (tail base, hips, belly, chest, neck) by computing each point's parameter along the full spiral path, then building a piecewise radius profile that grows from thin at the tail through the widest point at the belly and tapers again toward the neck, making sure the parameter values stay properly ordered along the path.

Now I'm setting up the paint function with a frecklepattern generator and starting to write the coat shader logic that uses the sweep position along the spine length to drive stripe placement...

Still writing coat coloring logic...

Now I'm figuring out the pectoral fin placement, extruding a thin plate from the body surface that sits flat against the side like a real fin, nudging it slightly outward from the body so it doesn't clip into the mesh.

I'm adding spiky brow cones above the eyes, then setting up the skeleton: a hip joint as root, a spine chain of four bones, and a tail chain of ten bones. Then I'm sweeping the body mesh across the back, core, and front bones with appropriate coloring.

For the body sweep I'm using 8 sides with faceted (non-smooth) shading to get a ridged look, and writing a small helper function for positioning points. Setting up imports from the builder library and defining cone-shaped knob geometry for the nodule loops along the body.

Now I'm placing knobs at 9 stations along the neck-to-tail range, each with 5 angular positions (0°, 60°, 300°, 120°, 240°), plus a spike at 180° using a slightly larger cone scaled to the hit radius. I'm figuring out total station counts across body and tail segments, and setting up the head/jaw joint hierarchy with jaw parented to head.

For the skull I'm building a scaled sphere (flattened and elongated) positioned forward and up from the head bone, painted with the coat color. Then I'm constructing the snout as a tapered rod running forward and slightly downward from the head, also bone-parented and colored to match the coat.

Now I'm adding crown spikes: placing a ring of seven tilted spikes around the top of the skull, oriented outward along the surface normal, plus one larger central spike at the crown point, all in the orange tone.
